questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive palmoplantar, nose & pinna pigmentation. Urine sample collected for Benedict’s test changes to black in the supernatant and the test gives greenish brown precipitate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alkaptonuria


Alkaptonuria is diagnosed based on the characteristic features of progressive pigmentation on the palms, nose, and pinna, along with urine turning black upon standing. This is caused by the accumulation of homogentisic acid, which oxidizes when exposed to air. The Benedict’s test is positive because homogentisic acid gives a greenish-brown precipitate and causes the supernatant to turn black. The enzyme deficient in this condition is homogentisate dioxygenase, also known as homogentisate oxidase.

 

In comparison, you should not forget these four important points about Phenylketonuria:

 

  1. The enzyme involved is phenylalanine hydroxylase.
  2. Symptoms include mental retardation.
  3. Hypopigmentation is often observed.
  4. The condition is associated with a mousy, musty odor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phenylketonuria: Phenylketonuria is characterized by the four key points mentioned above but does not present with black urine or progressive skin pigmentation.

 

Option C. Tyrosinemia type 2: Tyrosinemia type 2 is caused by a deficiency of tyrosine transaminase. Symptoms include mental retardation, painful corneal lesions, photophobia, and hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles. It does not cause urine to turn black or progressive pigmentation.

 

Option D. Argininosuccinic aciduria: This urea cycle disorder is caused by a deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase. It leads to developmental delays and the excretion of argininosuccinate in the urine, but it does not result in black urine or pigmentation.

 

Educational Objective:


Alkaptonuria is characterized by the accumulation of homogentisic acid, leading to black urine upon standing and progressive skin pigmentation, and is caused by a deficiency in homogentisate dioxygenase.

questions.stem: The type of enzyme inhibition in which Succinate dehydrogenase reaction is inhibited by malonate is an example of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Competitive


Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase through competitive inhibition. Malonate is a 3-carbon compound, while malate, an intermediate of the TCA cycle, is a 4-carbon compound. The key difference between the two is that malonate competes with succinate (which is the normal substrate for succinate dehydrogenase) for binding at the enzyme’s active site, thereby inhibiting the reaction. This type of inhibition is referred to as competitive inhibition. Malonate’s structure is similar to succinate, and because of this, it acts as a competitive inhibitor, blocking succinate from binding to the active site and halting the enzymatic reaction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Noncompetitive: Noncompetitive inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site, causing a change in the enzyme’s structure and reducing its activity. This is not the case with malonate and succinate dehydrogenase.

 

Option B. Uncompetitive: In uncompetitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex, not to the free enzyme, which is not how malonate works.

 

Option D. Allosteric: Allosteric inhibition involves the inhibitor binding to an allosteric site, which is distinct from the active site, modulating enzyme activity. Malonate does not act through an allosteric mechanism.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: A tRNA molecule that is supposed to carry cysteine (tRNAcys) is mischarged so that it actually carries alanine (ala-tRNAcys). Assuming no correction occurs, what will be the fate of this alanine residue during protein synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to an alanine codon

options.label: B
options.text: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon

options.label: C
options.text: It will remain attached to the tRNA as it cannot be used for protein synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: It will be chemically converted to cysteine by cellular enzymes

questions.answerText: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon.

 

The tRNA molecule in this case is mischarged, meaning it was supposed to carry cysteine but is now carrying alanine. During protein synthesis, the codon on the mRNA recognizes only the anticodon of the tRNA, not the amino acid attached to it. Therefore, if the anticodon matches the codon for cysteine, the alanine will still be incorporated into the protein at the position where cysteine should have been. The ribosome will not detect the error because it only recognizes the anticodon-codon match, not the amino acid itself.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It will be incorporated into a protein in response to an alanine codon:
This is incorrect because the anticodon of the tRNA is specific for cysteine, so it will bind to the codon for cysteine, not alanine.

 

Option C. It will remain attached to the tRNA as it cannot be used for protein synthesis: This is incorrect because the tRNA will still participate in protein synthesis, even though the wrong amino acid is attached. The ribosome only checks the codon-anticodon interaction.

 

Option D. It will be chemically converted to cysteine by cellular enzymes: There is no mechanism that chemically converts alanine back to cysteine once the tRNA has been mischarged.

 

Educational Objective:


When a tRNA molecule is mischarged, the amino acid attached (even if incorrect) will be incorporated into the protein according to the tRNA's anticodon, not the amino acid attached. Therefore, alanine will be added in response to a cysteine codon in this case.

questions.stem: The base sequence of the strand of DNA used as the template for transcription has the base sequence GATCTAC. What is the base sequence of RNA product?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) GUAGAUC

 

When determining the base sequence of the RNA product from a DNA template strand, the non-template (sense) strand is first generated, as it matches the RNA strand except for the substitution of uracil (U) for thymine (T).

 

The given DNA template strand is GATCTAC. The complementary non-template strand is generated by pairing the bases as follows:


G pairs with C, A pairs with T, T pairs with A, C pairs with G, etc.
This gives the non-template strand: CTAGATG.

 

From this, the RNA strand is generated by replacing thymine (T) with uracil (U):
The RNA sequence becomes GUAGAUC.

 

One key detail is that in the absence of direction indicators, it's assumed that the leftmost base corresponds to the 5' end, which aligns with the given answer choices.

 

Educational Objective:

 

To obtain the RNA sequence from a DNA template strand, first generate the complementary DNA strand (non-template), and then replace thymine (T) with uracil (U) in the RNA strand.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old baby was diagnosed with urea cycle disorder. Past history indicates the same disease in a previous baby who died at 1 year of age. What could be the rationale for feeding benzoic acid to subjects with a urea cycle enzyme defect?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion through glycine conjugate, hippuric acid

options.label: B
options.text: It provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion through N-acetylglucuronic acid conjugate kynurenine

options.label: D
options.text: It neutralizes ammonia in both blood and urine

questions.answerText: It provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion through glycine conjugate, hippuric acid
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) It provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion through glycine conjugate, hippuric acid


In urea cycle disorders, the body is unable to effectively eliminate nitrogen in the form of urea, leading to a toxic buildup of ammonia. Benzoic acid, or sodium benzoate, acts as an ammonia scavenging agent. When sodium benzoate enters the body, it combines with glycine, which contains one nitrogen atom. This reaction produces hippuric acid, which is then excreted in the urine, providing an alternative pathway to remove nitrogen from the body. Although phenylbutyrate is also used for this purpose (and is more effective, removing two nitrogen atoms), benzoic acid serves a similar function by helping to excrete nitrogen as hippuric acid.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. It provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion through N-acetylglucuronic acid conjugate kynurenine: This is incorrect because benzoic acid does not utilize this pathway for nitrogen excretion.

 

Option C. It inhibits adenylate deaminase: This is incorrect as benzoic acid does not have any inhibitory effects on adenylate deaminase.

 

Option D. It neutralizes ammonia in both blood and urine: This is incorrect. Benzoic acid does not neutralize ammonia but rather facilitates its excretion by converting it into hippuric acid via conjugation with glycine.

 

Educational Objective:


Benzoic acid provides an alternative route for nitrogen excretion by converting nitrogen to hippuric acid via conjugation with glycine, which is then excreted in the urine. This helps to lower ammonia levels in patients with urea cycle disorders.

questions.stemHtml: Which is the most probable diagnosis with reference to the below clinical features?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Familial Hypercholesterolemia


The image shows tendon xanthomas, which are deposits of cholesterol in the tendons, commonly seen in familial hypercholesterolemia. This condition is caused by a defect in the LDL receptor or apo B100, leading to elevated levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood. Familial hypercholesterolemia is characterized by these cholesterol deposits, which most frequently occur in the Achilles tendons, as shown in the image.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Familial Chylomicronemia: This is caused by a defect in lipoprotein lipase or apo C2 and leads to elevated triglycerides, not cholesterol. It is associated with pancreatitis rather than tendon xanthomas.

 

Option C. Abetalipoproteinemia: This condition results in low levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and phospholipids due to absent beta-lipoproteins. It presents with clinical features such as blindness due to retinal degeneration and the presence of acanthocytes (spiny projections on erythrocytes), which are not seen in this case.

 

Option D. Broad Beta Disease (Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia): This is a rare disorder caused by abnormal apo E, leading to the accumulation of remnant lipoproteins. While it involves elevated cholesterol, it is not associated with tendon xanthomas, making it less likely in this case.

 

Educational Objective:


Tendon xanthomas are a hallmark of familial hypercholesterolemia, a condition caused by defects in the LDL receptor or apo B100, leading to high cholesterol levels and cholesterol deposition in tendons.

questions.stem: Children with autism and other disorders with mental disability are often put on megavitamin supplements despite no scientific evidence of benefit. Although most vitamins are harmless in excess, merely being excreted in urine, vitamin A can be toxic. All of the following are symptoms of either chronic or acute vitamin A toxicity except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Xerophthalmia


The question asks for the symptom that is not associated with vitamin A toxicity. Xerophthalmia is a sign of vitamin A deficiency, not toxicity.

 

Vitamin A toxicity can result from either acute or chronic excessive intake and presents with various symptoms. 

 

Other Options:

 

Some of the symptoms of acute or chronic vitamin A toxicity include:

 

Option A. Dry pruritic skin: This is a known symptom of vitamin A toxicity.

 

Option B. Pseudo Tumour Cerebri: This is also associated with vitamin A toxicity, especially at higher doses.

 

Option C. Blurred Vision: Blurred vision can occur due to vitamin A toxicity, as it affects the nervous system and vision.

questions.stem: A neonatal examination was done in a newborn girl baby. On examination, the baby has blue eyes, blonde hair, and fair skin. Test result shows positive Guthrie test. All are true except:

options.label: C
options.text: White patch of hair due to tryptophan

questions.answerText: White patch of hair due to tryptophan
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) White patch of hair due to tryptophan

 

The baby’s presentation of blue eyes, blonde hair, fair skin, and a positive Guthrie test points to Phenylketonuria (PKU). PKU is due to a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to an accumulation of phenylalanine and its metabolites, including phenylacetate, in the urine. Hypopigmentation, as seen in the baby, is common because phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, which is necessary for melanin production.

 

All of the statements are true for PKU except for option C. The white patch of hair seen in PKU patients is due to tyrosine and melanin deficiency, not tryptophan.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Due to enzyme Phenylalanine Hydroxylase: This is true. PKU results from a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to the accumulation of phenylalanine.

 

Option B. Mental retardation present: This is true. If untreated, PKU can lead to mental retardation due to the toxic buildup of phenylalanine in the brain.

 

Option D. Phenylacetate positive in urine: This is true. Phenylacetate, along with other metabolites like phenylpyruvate and phenyl lactate, is excreted in the urine in PKU patients.

 

Educational Objective:


In Phenylketonuria, the deficiency in phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to hypopigmentation due to reduced tyrosine and melanin, and metabolites such as phenylacetate are present in the urine. The white patch of hair is due to tyrosine deficiency, not tryptophan.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with progressive muscle weakness, myopathy, and hepatomegaly. Upon investigation, a skeletal muscle biopsy reveals abnormal glycogen accumulation with very long outer branches. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anderson disease


The key finding in this case is the presence of abnormal glycogen with very long outer branches, which points to Anderson disease (also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type IV or amylopectinosis). In this condition, there is a deficiency of the enzyme branching enzyme (amylo-1,4 to 1,6-transglucosidase), leading to the accumulation of glycogen with fewer branch points and long outer branches, resembling a structure similar to amylopectin. This disease typically presents with hepatomegaly, progressive muscle weakness, and myopathy, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Von Gierke's disease: Von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) is characterized by hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis, but does not feature abnormal glycogen with long outer branches.

 

Option B. Pompe disease: Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) involves the accumulation of glycogen in lysosomes due to a deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase and presents with cardiomegaly, hypotonia, and muscle weakness but does not involve glycogen with long outer branches.

 

Option C. Cori disease: Cori disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type III) is caused by a deficiency in debranching enzyme, leading to the accumulation of limit dextrins (short outer branches of glycogen). This differs from Anderson disease, which is characterized by long outer branches.

 

Educational Objective:


Anderson disease is characterized by abnormal glycogen accumulation with long outer branches due to a deficiency of the branching enzyme, leading to progressive muscle weakness, myopathy, and hepatomegaly.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a true statement regarding the inhibitors in this graph?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibitor A decreases the affinity of enzyme for substrate

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibitor B decreases the affinity of enzyme for substrate

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibitor A decreases the Vmax of the enzyme

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibitors A and B have no effect on enzyme kinetic parameters

questions.answerText: Inhibitor A decreases the affinity of enzyme for substrate
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Inhibitor A decreases the affinity of enzyme for substrate

 

This graph represents a Lineweaver-Burk plot, which is commonly used to illustrate enzyme kinetics. In this plot:

 

Inhibitor A crosses the Y-axis, which is characteristic of a competitive inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor increases the Km (Michaelis constant), which results in a decreased affinity between the enzyme and the substrate, but Vmax remains unchanged.

 

Inhibitor B crosses the X-axis, characteristic of a non-competitive inhibitor. Non-competitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax but do not affect the Km, meaning the enzyme's affinity for the substrate remains unchanged.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inhibitor B decreases the affinity of enzyme for substrate: This is incorrect because non-competitive inhibitors (Inhibitor B) do not change the affinity for the substrate (i.e., Km remains the same).

 

Option C. Inhibitor A decreases the Vmax of the enzyme: This is incorrect because competitive inhibitors (Inhibitor A) do not affect the Vmax; they only increase the Km, affecting the enzyme's affinity for the substrate.

 

Option D. Inhibitors A and B have no effect on enzyme kinetic parameters: This is incorrect as both Inhibitor A and Inhibitor B affect enzyme kinetics. Inhibitor A increases Km, and Inhibitor B decreases Vmax.

 

Educational Objectives:


In competitive inhibition, Km increases (decreasing affinity), while Vmax remains unchanged. In non-competitive inhibition, Vmax decreases, but Km remains unchanged.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents with enlarged, yellow-orange tonsils and reports intermittent episodes of neuropathy. Which of the following is a characteristic finding in his plasma lipoprotein profile?

options.label: C
options.text: Absent or extremely low HDL cholesterol

questions.answerText: Absent or extremely low HDL cholesterol
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Absent or extremely low HDL cholesterol


The presentation of enlarged, yellow-orange tonsils is a classic feature of Tangier disease, which is caused by a mutation in the ABCA1 gene. This mutation leads to a deficiency or absence of HDL cholesterol (also known as alpha-lipoprotein). Tangier disease is characterized by very low or absent HDL cholesterol levels, which results in the accumulation of cholesterol in various tissues, causing the yellow-orange discoloration of the tonsils. Patients also experience neuropathy and other symptoms related to lipid metabolism disorders.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Elevated HDL cholesterol: This is incorrect, as HDL cholesterol is absent or extremely low in Tangier disease.

 

Option B. Elevated LDL cholesterol: Tangier disease does not result in elevated LDL cholesterol. The primary abnormality is related to HDL cholesterol.

 

Option D. Elevated chylomicrons: This is not characteristic of Tangier disease. Elevated chylomicrons are seen in conditions like familial chylomicronemia.

 

Educational Objective:


Tangier disease is characterized by the absence or extremely low levels of HDL cholesterol and presents with yellow-orange tonsils, neuropathy, and lipid metabolism abnormalities due to an ABCA1 mutation.

questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old female presents with chronic fatigue, easy bruising, and hepatosplenomegaly. On bone marrow examination, cells with a characteristic appearance as shown in the image below are observed. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Beta Gluco-cerebrosidase


The image and clinical presentation are characteristic of Gaucher’s disease, which is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme beta-glucocerebrosidase. The presence of Gaucher cells—enlarged macrophages with a crumpled tissue paper appearance, as seen in the image—is a hallmark of this disease. Gaucher disease leads to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in various tissues, particularly within the bone marrow, spleen, and liver, leading to symptoms such as hepatosplenomegaly, easy bruising, and chronic fatigue due to pancytopenia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. α-L-Iduronidase: This enzyme is deficient in Hurler syndrome, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by developmental delays, coarse facial features, and corneal clouding, but it is not associated with the appearance of Gaucher cells.

 

Option B. Hexosaminidase A: A deficiency in hexosaminidase A causes Tay-Sachs disease, which presents with neurological symptoms like developmental delay and seizures, but not the characteristic cells shown in the image.

 

Option C. Alpha-Gluco-cerebrosidase: This enzyme is not associated with any known metabolic disorder. The correct enzyme involved in Gaucher disease is beta-glucocerebrosidase.

 

Educational Objective:


Gaucher’s disease is caused by a deficiency in beta-glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of glucocerebroside and characteristic Gaucher cells in tissues. This manifests as hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue, and easy bruising.

questions.stem: A newborn presents with a distinctive sweet odor in the urine and shows signs of poor feeding and lethargy within a few days after birth. Which of the following biochemical abnormalities are characteristic of this infant's condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of α-keto acids in the urine

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of homogentisic acid in urine

questions.answerText: Presence of α-keto acids in the urine
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Presence of α-keto acids in the urine


The distinctive sweet odor in the urine is a hallmark of Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD). This metabolic disorder is caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, leading to the accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, and valine) and their corresponding α-keto acids in the blood and urine. These metabolites are responsible for the sweet or maple syrup-like odor in the urine and the neurological symptoms observed, such as poor feeding and lethargy shortly after birth.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. An elevation in serum phenylalanine: This is characteristic of Phenylketonuria (PKU), not MSUD.

 

Option C. Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans: This occurs in mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler and Hunter syndromes) and is not related to MSUD.

 

Option D. Presence of homogentisic acid in urine: This is seen in Alkaptonuria, a different metabolic disorder, not MSUD.

 

Educational Objectives:


In Maple Syrup Urine Disease, there is an accumulation of branched-chain amino acids and their corresponding α-keto acids, which can be detected in the blood and urine, producing a sweet, maple syrup-like odor.

questions.stem: In a study on post-transcriptional gene silencing, an enzyme that processes precursor RNA into short double-stranded fragments was inhibited, leading to gene upregulation. Which of the following enzymes is inhibited?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dicer


Post-transcriptional gene silencing, also known as RNA interference (RNAi) or the gene knockdown technique, involves enzymes that process precursor RNA into short double-stranded fragments. When these enzymes are inhibited, gene upregulation occurs. The key enzymes involved in RNA interference are Drosha, Parsha, Dicer, and other endonucleases. Among these, Dicer is the enzyme that processes the precursor RNA, so its inhibition leads to gene upregulation.

 

DNA polymerase is involved in DNA synthesis, Ribonuclease P cuts tRNA, and RNA polymerase II is involved in RNA transcription, but none of these participate in RNA interference.

 

In RNA interference, Dicer processes RNA, forming the RISC complex, which, along with microRNA, inhibits target mRNA, leading to gene silencing.

 

Other Options:


Option A. DNA polymerase: Involved in DNA synthesis, not RNA interference.

 

Option B. Ribonuclease P: A ribozyme that cuts tRNA, not involved in RNA interference.

 

Option D. RNA polymerase II: Involved in RNA synthesis but not part of RNA interference.

 

Educational Objective:


Dicer processes precursor RNA into double-stranded fragments in RNA interference, and its inhibition leads to gene upregulation.

questions.stem: A molecular biologist is preparing to amplify a specific DNA segment using an enzyme-catalyzed thermocycler-based reaction. Which of the following components, if not included in the reaction mixture, will not affect the amplification process?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) DNA ligase


The thermocycler-based reaction mentioned refers to PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), which requires several essential components: double-stranded DNA (to be amplified), two primers (one for each strand), Taq polymerase, dNTPs (deoxynucleotide triphosphates), and magnesium ions (Mg2+). These five components are critical for the PCR process.

 

DNA ligase, however, is not required for PCR. This enzyme is involved in joining DNA fragments, typically during DNA repair or replication, but it is not involved in the amplification process.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Taq polymerase: Essential for synthesizing new DNA strands during PCR.

 

Option C. DNA primers & Magnesium ions (Mg2+): Primers are required to start the DNA synthesis, and Mg2+ is a cofactor for Taq polymerase.

 

Option D. dNTPs (deoxynucleotide triphosphates): These are the building blocks needed for DNA synthesis in PCR.

 

Educational Objective:


DNA ligase is not required for PCR and its absence will not affect the DNA amplification process.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female on a strict vegetarian diet presents with fatigue, weakness, and pallor. Blood work shows macrocytic anemia. Lab investigations reveal elevated levels of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. A specific metabolic blockade due to a vitamin deficiency is suspected to underlie her condition, leading to a "trapped" state of a particular molecule. Which of the following combinations best describes the deficient vitamin and the "trapped" molecule in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Vitamin B12 and 5-methyl THF

 

Presenting with fatigue, weakness, and macrocytic anemia while on a strict vegetarian diet, points toward vitamin B12 deficiency. A vegetarian diet often lacks sufficient B12, which can lead to macrocytic anemia. The lab findings of elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid further confirm B12 deficiency.

 

In B12 deficiency, there is a phenomenon known as the folate trap. Normally, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-methyl THF) is converted to tetrahydrofolate (THF), the active form of folate, but this reaction requires vitamin B12. In the absence of B12, 5-methyl THF gets "trapped" because it cannot be converted to its active form. Therefore, the deficient vitamin is B12, and the trapped molecule is 5-methyl THF.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vitamin B6 and Pyridoxal phosphate: Vitamin B6 deficiency is not related to this case, and Pyridoxal phosphate is involved in different metabolic pathways.

 

Option C. Vitamin B12 and 10-formyl THF: 10-formyl THF is not involved in the folate trap mechanism.

 

Option D. Folic acid and THF: Folic acid deficiency can cause anemia, but this case is specific to B12 deficiency and the trapping of 5-methyl THF.

 

Educational Objective:


In vitamin B12 deficiency, 5-methyl THF becomes trapped, leading to macrocytic anemia and elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy came with complaints of anemia, weakness, and a low weight-to-height ratio for his age profile. On examination, the urine sample shows elevated levels of orotic acid. Further study reveals low uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase activity. What can be the best treatment to administer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Uridine


The patient presents with anemia, weakness, and a low weight-to-height ratio, along with elevated orotic acid in the urine. Elevated orotic acid can occur in two conditions: orotic aciduria and ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. In this case, the study reveals low uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase activity, which points towards orotic aciduria rather than OTC deficiency.

 

In orotic aciduria, UMP is not synthesized due to a defect in UMP synthase. The best treatment for this condition is administering uridine, which helps bypass the metabolic block. Once uridine is provided, the body can synthesize cytidine (C) and deoxythymidine (D), as the enzymes for these conversions are not deficient in orotic aciduria.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adenine: Not involved in the correction of UMP synthase deficiency.

 

Option C. Hypoxanthine: This is a purine precursor, irrelevant in the context of pyrimidine synthesis and UMP deficiency.

 

Option D. Thymidine: Although involved in DNA synthesis, it is not the appropriate treatment for UMP synthase deficiency.

 

Educational Objective:


The best treatment for orotic aciduria, due to low UMP synthase activity, is administering uridine, which helps synthesize the necessary pyrimidines.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with pallor and cyanosis with the following presentation (as seen in the image). This condition is most probably due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vitamin B12 deficiency

 

The image shows knuckle pigmentation, which is a characteristic sign of Vitamin B12 deficiency. This pigmentation can also be seen in Addison’s disease, but in this case, it is more indicative of Vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to increased production of oxidants, such as homocysteine, which depletes glutathione, an antioxidant. Glutathione usually prevents unnecessary melanin formation, but when it is depleted, tyrosinase is activated, leading to increased melanin production and subsequent pigmentation on the knuckles.

 

Other associated signs of Vitamin B12 deficiency include oral mucosal pigmentation, recurrent angular stomatitis, and other skin and hair changes like polymorphic cutaneous eruptions and dry, lusterless hair.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Folic acid deficiency: Folic acid deficiency can cause macrocytic anemia but does not typically present with knuckle pigmentation.

 

Option B. Iron deficiency anemia: Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with pallor and fatigue, but knuckle pigmentation is not a feature.

 

Option D. Thalassemia: Thalassemia leads to microcytic anemia and may show different symptoms, but knuckle pigmentation is not a hallmark of the condition.

 

Educational Objective:


Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to knuckle pigmentation, which is often an overlooked but reversible sign of the condition.

questions.stem: A bodybuilder starts eating raw eggs for protein. He developed fatigue during moderate exercise. The doctor prescribes a vitamin. Which enzyme will be negatively affected in him?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pyruvate Carboxylase


The consumption of raw eggs can lead to biotin (vitamin B7) deficiency, as raw eggs contain avidin, which binds to biotin and prevents its absorption. Biotin is crucial for carboxylase enzymes, including Pyruvate Carboxylase, which is involved in gluconeogenesis. In biotin deficiency, pyruvate carboxylase is negatively affected, leading to potential hypoglycemic attacks, particularly in individuals engaging in moderate exercise like the bodybuilder in the case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucose 6 Phosphatase: This enzyme is involved in glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis but is not affected by biotin deficiency. It is related to Von Gierke's disease and is located in the endoplasmic reticulum.

 

Option C. PEPCK (Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase): While involved in gluconeogenesis, PEPCK requires GTP, not biotin, and is not a carboxylase enzyme.

 

Option D. Glycogen Phosphorylase: This enzyme is involved in glycogenolysis and requires vitamin B6, not biotin (B7).

 

Educational Objective:


Biotin (B7) deficiency, caused by consuming raw eggs, affects carboxylase enzymes like pyruvate carboxylase, which plays a key role in gluconeogenesis, potentially leading to hypoglycemia.

questions.stemHtml: The point X shown in the following enzyme kinetic plot represents which of the following value?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) -1/Km

 

The provided graph is a Lineweaver-Burk plot, which is a double reciprocal plot of enzyme kinetics. The x-axis of this plot represents 1/[S] (the reciprocal of substrate concentration), and the y-axis represents 1/V (the reciprocal of reaction velocity). The point X is located on the negative side of the x-axis. In the Lineweaver-Burk plot, the intercept on the negative x-axis corresponds to -1/Km. Therefore, the value of point X is -1/Km.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Km: The value of Km is not directly shown on this graph. The point X represents -1/Km, not Km itself.

 

Option C. Km/Vmax: This is not represented by point X on the graph.

 

Option D. 1/Vmax: This value is represented by the y-intercept, not by point X.

questions.stem: In glycogen metabolism, a metabolically active important enzyme found in the liver is converted from its inactive dephosphorylated state to its active phosphorylated state. Which of the following is true about this enzyme:

options.label: C
options.text: More commonly seen in fasting state than in fed state

options.label: D
options.text: Always activated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase

questions.answerText: More commonly seen in fasting state than in fed state
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) More commonly seen in fasting state than in fed state

 

In glycogen metabolism, when an enzyme is described as being active in its phosphorylated state, it refers to a catabolic enzyme. Catabolic enzymes are generally activated by phosphorylation and are more active in the fasting state compared to the fed state.

 

This is true. Catabolic enzymes such as those involved in glycogen breakdown are more active during the fasting state when the body requires glucose from glycogen stores.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phosphorylation sometimes activates the enzyme: This is incorrect. In the case of catabolic enzymes like glycogen phosphorylase, phosphorylation always activates the enzyme, not sometimes.

 

Option B. Catecholamines directly stimulate it: Catecholamines (like epinephrine) do play a role in stimulating phosphorylation, but they do not directly stimulate the enzyme. Catecholamines work through a signaling cascade that leads to enzyme phosphorylation.

 

Option D. Always activated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase: While cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) plays a major role in activating enzymes by phosphorylation, not all enzymes in glycogen metabolism are activated exclusively by PKA. However, it is a key player in the activation process.

 

Educational Objective:


Catabolic enzymes in glycogen metabolism are more commonly seen in the fasting state, and their activation is closely linked to phosphorylation, especially through pathways involving cAMP and catecholamines.

questions.stem: The tensile strength of collagen fibers is provided by its triple helical structure, which can be most accurately described as which of the following levels of protein structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Quaternary

 

Collagen's tensile strength is due to its triple helical structure, which consists of three alpha chains. This type of structure falls under the quaternary level of protein structure because quaternary structure involves two or more polypeptide chains interacting to form a functional protein. In the case of collagen, the three alpha chains form a stable triple helix, which gives collagen its characteristic strength.

 

The difference between tertiary and quaternary structure is that tertiary structure involves a single polypeptide chain folded into a functional form, while quaternary structure involves the interaction of multiple polypeptide chains. For example, myoglobin only has a tertiary structure as it consists of one polypeptide chain, whereas collagen has a quaternary structure due to its three interacting chains.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Primary: The primary structure refers to the sequence of amino acids in a single polypeptide chain, which is not sufficient to describe the collagen's triple helical structure.
 

Option B. Secondary: The secondary structure includes alpha helices and beta sheets formed by hydrogen bonding within a single polypeptide chain, but it does not fully describe the three-chain structure of collagen.
 

Option C. Tertiary: Tertiary structure involves the folding of a single polypeptide chain into a functional form. While collagen's alpha chains do fold, its overall structure is quaternary because it involves multiple chains.

 

Educational Objective:


Collagen's triple helical structure, formed by three alpha chains, is an example of quaternary structure, providing it with its tensile strength.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient who has consumed street food over the past few days visits a clinic reporting persistent vomiting for the last 3 days. Despite being unable to eat or drink much, his blood glucose level was found to be in the normal range. Which organ primarily played a significant role in maintaining his blood glucose in this situation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Liver

 

In this situation, the patient has not consumed food for the past three days due to persistent vomiting, yet his blood glucose levels remain normal. The organ primarily responsible for maintaining normal blood glucose levels in this condition is the liver.

 

The liver plays a crucial role in glucose homeostasis through two key processes:

 

  1. Glycogenolysis: The breakdown of glycogen stores to release glucose into the blood. This process occurs early in fasting.
  2. Gluconeogenesis: The synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, such as amino acids and lactate, which becomes the dominant process during prolonged fasting or starvation.

 

Muscle tissue does not release glucose into the blood because it lacks the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase. Similarly, adipose tissue and kidneys are not the primary organs responsible for maintaining blood glucose during fasting or vomiting.

 

Educational Objective:


The liver is responsible for maintaining blood glucose levels during periods of fasting or vomiting by utilizing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: A patient with Type I Diabetes presented with complaints of polyuria. His RQ (Respiratory Quotient) was found to be decreased compared to a normal person. Which of the following will occur in his body?

options.label: D
options.text: Increased conversion of FA (Fatty Acids) to Acetyl CoA

questions.answerText: Increased conversion of FA (Fatty Acids) to Acetyl CoA
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Increased conversion of FA to Acetyl CoA
 

In a diabetic patient, particularly one with Type I Diabetes, the metabolic state is similar to fasting or starvation. In these situations, the body shifts from using carbohydrates to using fats as the primary fuel source, which leads to a decreased

 

Respiratory Quotient (RQ).

 

In diabetes, catabolic pathways are activated, such as:

 

Lipolysis (breakdown of fats)

 

Beta oxidation (conversion of fatty acids to Acetyl CoA)

 

Ketone body synthesis

 

Gluconeogenesis (generation of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources) As a result, there is an increased conversion of fatty acids to Acetyl CoA (beta oxidation) in diabetic patients. Additionally, excess Acetyl CoA in the liver contributes to fat synthesis in the liver, leading to increased triglycerides, cholesterol, and sometimes fatty liver.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Glycogenesis in muscle: This is incorrect because glycogenesis (the storage of glucose as glycogen) is not activated in a catabolic state like diabetes.

 

Option B. Increased protein synthesis: In a diabetic or fasting state, protein synthesis is decreased, and instead, proteolysis (breakdown of proteins) may occur.

 

Option C. Decreased cholesterol synthesis: Cholesterol synthesis is actually increased in diabetic patients due to excess Acetyl CoA, so this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:


In Type I Diabetes, the body shifts to using fatty acids as the primary fuel, leading to an increased conversion of fatty acids to Acetyl CoA through beta oxidation.

questions.stem: A male child presented with coarse facies, protuberant abdomen, frontal head enlargement, thickening of cardiac valves, hepatosplenomegaly, hearing impairment. There was no corneal clouding seen. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hunter’s disease


Presents with coarse facial features, protuberant abdomen, frontal head enlargement, thickened cardiac valves, hepatosplenomegaly, and hearing impairment. The key distinguishing feature is the absence of corneal clouding.

 

This presentation is characteristic of Hunter’s disease, a mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS type II), which is an X-linked recessive disorder. Hunter's disease shares many features with Hurler's disease (MPS type I), but corneal clouding is absent in Hunter's disease, making it the correct diagnosis here.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hurler’s disease: Hurler's disease also presents with similar features (coarse facies, organomegaly, etc.), but it is associated with corneal clouding, which is absent in this patient.

 

Option C. Fragile X syndrome: This is a genetic disorder associated with intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, and other symptoms, but it does not match the presentation here.

 

Option D. Tay Sach’s disease: Tay-Sachs disease is a neurodegenerative disorder and does not involve the physical features described, such as coarse facial features or organomegaly.

 

Educational Objectives:


The absence of corneal clouding along with the other described features strongly suggests a diagnosis of Hunter’s disease (MPS II).

questions.stem: A 12-month-old infant was brought to the hospital with complaints of screaming after feeding. Removal of milk from the diet did not alleviate the symptoms. All the growth parameters of the child were normal. A liver biopsy analysis reported no enzyme deficiency. Later, a detailed feeding analysis revealed that screaming bouts occurred every time the child was given fruit puree or fruit juice, which immediately caused gas formation and a distended abdomen. Most likely, a biopsy of the patient's intestinal tissue would reveal a deficiency or defect of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) GLUT 5


The infant experienced symptoms of gas formation and a distended abdomen specifically after consuming fruit puree or fruit juice, indicating an issue with fructose metabolism. GLUT 5 is the transporter responsible for the absorption of fructose in the intestine. The fact that the symptoms are triggered by fruit consumption and there was no enzyme deficiency in the liver biopsy suggests that the problem lies in the intestinal absorption of fructose, which points to a GLUT 5 deficiency.

 

This is not a case of lactose intolerance (which would involve lactase deficiency) or hereditary fructose intolerance (which would involve enzyme deficiencies detected in the liver). Therefore, the Ans. is GLUT 5, as it is specifically related to fructose transport.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. GLUT 2: GLUT 2 is involved in glucose transport, not fructose transport.

 

Option B. Lactase: Lactase deficiency leads to lactose intolerance, which is unrelated to the symptoms described.

 

Option D. SGLT 1: SGLT 1 is responsible for glucose and galactose absorption, not fructose absorption.

 

Educational Objective:


The child’s symptoms of gas and abdominal distension after consuming fruit are likely due to a defect in GLUT 5, the transporter responsible for fructose absorption.

questions.stem: A strange rash on a child from a refugee camp signals starvation. His parents recall that two of his siblings have the same rash and suffer from a condition known as Hartnup disease. Patients with this condition have a problem absorbing neutral amino acids from their intestines. The doctor told the parents that in this disease, rashes are probably caused by pellagra, which is brought on by niacin deficiency. Which of the following is the reason behind niacin deficiency in Hartnup disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Deficiency of tryptophan

 

In Hartnup disease, patients have an issue absorbing neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, from the intestines and also reabsorbing them in the kidneys. Tryptophan is a precursor for niacin (vitamin B3), which is essential to prevent pellagra. Due to the loss of tryptophan in Hartnup disease, the body cannot synthesize adequate niacin, leading to a niacin deficiency, which in turn causes pellagra-like rashes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Deficiency of phenylalanine: Phenylalanine is not the cause of niacin deficiency in Hartnup disease.

 

Option B. Deficiency of leucine: Leucine is another neutral amino acid but does not directly affect niacin synthesis.

 

Option D. Deficiency of glycine: Glycine is not involved in niacin synthesis and is not primarily affected in Hartnup disease.

 

Educational Objective:


The niacin deficiency in Hartnup disease is due to the loss of tryptophan, which is a precursor for niacin synthesis.

questions.stem: The main complaint of a 40-year-old guy is that he experiences occasional pain in leg and arm during exercise. The cardiovascular illness on his father's side of the family is significant, but not on his mother's side. A physical examination identifies bilateral tendon xanthomas and xanthelasmas. A high LDL/HDL ratio and a cholesterol level of 350 mg/dL are shown by a plasma lipid profile. Simvastatin is prescribed, along with guidelines for dietary changes. Clinical observations made in this patient are most likely the result of inadequate production of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) ApoB-100 receptors

 

Patient presents with signs consistent with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), a condition characterized by high cholesterol levels (LDL > 350 mg/dL), xanthomas, and a family history of cardiovascular disease. Familial hypercholesterolemia results from a defect in the LDL receptor or ApoB-100, which is the ligand for the LDL receptor.

 

In this case, since the LDL receptor defect is not listed in the options, the next most likely cause is a defect in ApoB-100, which impairs the body's ability to remove LDL from the bloodstream, leading to high levels of circulating LDL and cholesterol. This condition is classified as Type 2a hyperlipoproteinemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lethicin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT): This enzyme is involved in HDL metabolism, but its deficiency leads to low HDL, not high LDL, and is not linked to xanthomas.

 

Option C. Fatty acyl-CoA synthetase: This enzyme is involved in fatty acid metabolism, but its deficiency is not associated with the symptoms of familial hypercholesterolemia.

 

Option D. VLDL from LDL: This is incorrect because VLDL is converted to LDL, but the issue here is with LDL clearance, not VLDL production.

questions.stemHtml: When a nucleotide shown in the figure below is inserted in a growing DNA chain during a PCR reaction, what will happen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) DNA synthesis stops

 

The nucleotide shown in the figure is a dideoxynucleotide. In the structure, you can see that both the 2' and 3' hydroxyl (OH) groups are absent. Normally, in deoxyribose (found in DNA), there is an OH group at the 3' position that is essential for forming the phosphodiester bond with the next nucleotide in the growing DNA chain. In dideoxyribose, this OH group is missing at the 3' position, preventing further extension of the DNA chain.

 

Therefore, when a dideoxynucleotide is incorporated into a growing DNA strand during a PCR reaction, DNA synthesis stops, as the lack of a 3' OH prevents further nucleotide additions.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Fluorescence occurs: This is unrelated to dideoxynucleotides. Fluorescence might be seen in sequencing methods, but it's not directly caused by dideoxynucleotides.

 

Option C. DNA synthesis is faster: This is incorrect. Dideoxynucleotides halt DNA synthesis rather than accelerating it.

 

Option D. DNA synthesis is slower: While dideoxynucleotides stop DNA synthesis, they do not just slow it down. They completely halt the process.

 

Educational Objective:


Incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide during DNA synthesis results in termination of the DNA strand, as no further nucleotides can be added.

questions.stem: A graduate student wants to prepare a genomic library of a human cell line in Escherichia coli cells. For this, she needs to cut plasmid DNA of E. coli as well as human cell DNA with a restriction enzyme that is always known to cut DNA at a palindromic sequence. Which of the following DNA sequences is palindromic in nature that this enzyme might recognize?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) GTGCAC

 

Restriction enzymes typically recognize and cut palindromic sequences in DNA. A palindromic sequence is one where the sequence of nucleotides reads the same in both directions (5' to 3') on complementary strands.

 

This sequence is palindromic. If you write the complementary strand, you get CACGTG, and when reading both strands from 5' to 3', they mirror each other.

Therefore, the correct palindromic sequence is GTGCAC.

 

Educational Objectives:


Restriction enzymes recognize palindromic sequences in DNA, and for this example, the sequence GTGCAC fits the criteria of a palindrome.



ore, the correct palindromic sequence is GTGCAC. Educational Objectives:Restriction enzymes recognize palindromic sequences in DNA, and for this example, the sequence GTGCAC fits the criteria of a palindrome.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child displaying bronchitis, persistent cough, and growth failure presents to a doctor. The mother reports that the child has light-colored and foul-smelling feces due to persistent diarrhea. Which of the following vitamin treatments should be taken into consideration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Answer: A. Vitamin A

 

A 2-year-old child with:

  • Bronchitis, persistent cough
  • Growth failure
  • Light-colored, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea)
  • Persistent diarrhea

 

These findings suggest malabsorption, likely due to Cystic Fibrosis (CF), a common genetic condition in children that affects exocrine glands, leading to:

  • Thick mucus in lungs → recurrent respiratory infections
  • Pancreatic insufficiency → malabsorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
  • Steatorrhea (fatty, foul-smelling stools)

 

Vitamin A:

  • It is fat-soluble → poorly absorbed in pancreatic enzyme deficiency
  • Vitamin A deficiency causes:
    • Impaired immunity
    • Increased risk of respiratory infections
    • Vision problems (especially night blindness)
    • Delayed growth

Supplementation is often needed in children with CF to prevent complications.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. Vitamin C

  • Water-soluble
  • Deficiency → scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing)
  • Absorbed normally in CF → not a priority

 

Option C. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine)

  • Water-soluble
  • Deficiency → beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff (mostly in alcoholics or severe malnutrition)
  • Not typically deficient in CF

 

Option D. Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)

  • Water-soluble
  • Deficiency → angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • Again, not a key concern in fat malabsorption

 

Educational Objective:

In cases of steatorrhea, where fat absorption is impaired, deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins like Vitamin A should be considered. Vitamin A deficiency can lead to recurrent infections, as seen in this child.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is on a regular prescription of warfarin for the treatment of blood clots. She is planning to become pregnant, so her physician is considering changing her medication to prevent fetal warfarin syndrome, vitamin K deficiency, and potential bleeding episodes in the infant. What biochemical activity might be deficient in the infant if her medication is continued?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) γ-Carboxylation of glutamate
 

The patient is on warfarin, which inhibits vitamin K. During pregnancy, continuing warfarin can cause fetal warfarin syndrome, resulting in vitamin K deficiency in the fetus, leading to hemorrhage and potential bleeding episodes.

 

γ-Carboxylation of glutamate is a key biochemical activity that is dependent on vitamin K. This process is crucial for the function of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. If warfarin continues to inhibit vitamin K, γ-carboxylation will be impaired, potentially causing bleeding issues in the fetus.

 

Thus, if the mother continues taking warfarin during pregnancy, the infant may experience a deficiency in γ-carboxylation of glutamate, leading to clotting issues and bleeding episodes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydroxylation of proline is not affected by warfarin. This process is involved in collagen synthesis and is dependent on vitamin C and iron, not vitamin K.

 

Option B. Glucuronidation of bilirubin is a liver function process unrelated to warfarin or vitamin K.

 

Option D. Reduction of glutathione is catalyzed by glutathione reductase, which depends on vitamin B2 (riboflavin), not vitamin K.

 

Educational Objective:


Warfarin inhibits vitamin K, which is essential for γ-carboxylation of glutamate in clotting factors. Continuing warfarin during pregnancy could lead to fetal warfarin syndrome and a deficiency in this critical biochemical activity, potentially causing hemorrhage in the infant.

questions.stem: A number of proteins are involved in moving iron from intestinal mucosal cells or liver storage into the circulation and delivery to other organs. Which of the following proteins binds to particular cell surface receptors to transfer iron to tissues?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Transferrin

 

Transferrin is the protein responsible for binding to specific cell surface receptors and transferring iron to tissues. After iron (Fe²⁺) is absorbed into the intestinal mucosal cells, it is stored as ferritin. When iron is released into the circulation, it binds to transferrin, which transports iron through the bloodstream and delivers it to tissues via transferrin receptors on cell surfaces.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ferritin stores iron within cells and is not involved in transporting iron in the bloodstream.

 

Option B. Ferredoxin is involved in electron transport and is not related to iron transport.

 

Option C. Hemosiderin is an iron-storage complex that forms when ferritin is in excess and is not involved in transporting iron.

 

Educational Objective:


Transferrin is the protein responsible for binding and transferring iron to tissues through specific cell surface receptors.

questions.stemHtml: An 18-year-old girl presents to a clinic with yellow discoloration (jaundice) of the skin, difficulty speaking, poor articulation, and lack of coordination. Ophthalmologic examination shows rusty-brown deposits in the corneas of the eyes as shown in the picture below. Examination of her blood and urine revealed higher than average levels of free copper. She is suffering from which of the following diseases?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Wilson disease

 

The rusty-brown deposits seen in the corneas are known as Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings, which are characteristic of Wilson disease. This is a genetic disorder where there is impaired copper metabolism, leading to the accumulation of copper in various tissues, including the liver, brain, and eyes.

 

Other symptoms include jaundice, neurological symptoms such as difficulty speaking, poor coordination, and increased levels of free copper in the blood and urine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Keshan’s disease: This is related to selenium deficiency, not copper metabolism.

 

Option C. Menke disease: This is a genetic disorder characterized by copper deficiency, not excess copper.

 

Option D. Wernicke encephalopathy: This is related to vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, commonly seen in alcoholics, and does not involve copper accumulation.

 

Educational Objective:


Wilson disease is characterized by copper accumulation, with key signs like Kayser-Fleischer rings, jaundice, and neurological symptoms.

questions.stem: A teenager suffering from the deficiency of muscle phosphorylase is getting examined by a rubber ball squeezing test while exercising her forearm. Which of the following statements will be true for this patient compared to a normal person?

options.label: B
options.text: ↑ blood glucose in the blood drawn from the exercising forearm vein

options.label: C
options.text: ↑ blood lactate in the blood drawn from the exercising forearm vein

options.label: D
options.text: Relatively ↓ blood lactate in the blood drawn from the exercising forearm vein

questions.answerText: Relatively ↓ blood lactate in the blood drawn from the exercising forearm vein
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Relatively ↓ blood lactate in the blood drawn from the exercising forearm vein

 

The case describes a teenager with muscle phosphorylase deficiency, being tested by repeated handgrip exercise using a rubber ball squeeze test. This is a classic clinical scenario pointing to:

 

McArdle Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V)

  • Deficiency: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase)
  • Consequence: Impaired glycogen breakdown in muscle → ↓ glucose-6-phosphate for glycolysis
  • Result: ↓ ATP → muscle cramps, fatigue, and exercise intolerance
  • Classic finding: No rise in lactate during anaerobic exercise (due to lack of glycolytic substrate)

 

Rubber ball squeezing test:

  • In normal individuals:
    • Exercise → glycogenolysis → glycolysis → ↑ pyruvate → ↑ lactate in blood from exercising forearm
  • In McArdle disease:
    • No glycogenolysis → no substrate for glycolysis → no increase in lactate

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. Exercise endurance

  • Would be reduced, not increased — patients fatigue quickly due to lack of ATP.

 

Option B. ↑ blood glucose

  • Not seen in localized forearm blood during exercise. Also, the issue is with glycogen breakdown in muscle, not systemic glucose levels.

 

Option C. ↑ blood lactate

  • This is what you'd expect in a normal person, not in someone with McArdle disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In McArdle's disease, due to the deficiency of muscle phosphorylase, blood lactate levels do not increase during exercise, leading to relatively decreased blood lactate in comparison to a normal individual.

questions.stem: A young man goes to a clinic and tells the doctor that he feels unwell after eating dairy products, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. When he stops eating dairy, these problems go away. To manage his symptoms, he could benefit from a supplement containing which of the following enzymes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) β-Galactosidase

 

The patient's symptoms of gas, bloating, and diarrhea after consuming dairy products are indicative of lactose intolerance, which results from a deficiency in the enzyme lactase. Lactase is required to break down lactose, the sugar found in milk and other dairy products. When lactase is deficient, lactose is not properly digested, leading to gastrointestinal symptoms.

 

Lactase is also known as β-galactosidase, and supplementation with this enzyme can help alleviate symptoms by improving lactose digestion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. α-amylase: This enzyme breaks down starch, not lactose, and is irrelevant in this case.

 

Option B. α-Galactosidase: This enzyme helps digest complex carbohydrates found in legumes and vegetables, not lactose.

 

Option D. β-Galactocerebrosidase: This enzyme is deficient in Krabbe’s disease, a lysosomal storage disorder, and is unrelated to lactose metabolism.

 

Educational Objectives:


The enzyme lactase, also known as β-galactosidase, is deficient in individuals with lactose intolerance. Supplementation with β-galactosidase can help manage symptoms when consuming dairy products.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who drank too much alcohol fell in the street. He was quickly taken to the hospital. What is the first-line treatment to be given to this patient in the ER?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Vitamin B1

 

In the case of an alcoholic patient, the first-line treatment should be Vitamin B1 (thiamine). This is because chronic alcohol use often leads to thiamine deficiency, which is necessary for the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA via the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Without sufficient thiamine, pyruvate gets converted to lactate, which can lead to lactic acidosis.

 

If glucose is administered first, it can exacerbate the situation by increasing the production of pyruvate, which, due to thiamine deficiency, will not be converted to acetyl-CoA but instead further contribute to lactic acidosis. Therefore, thiamine (Vitamin B1) must be given before glucose to prevent worsening lactic acidosis in alcoholic patients.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Glucose: Administering glucose first without thiamine can worsen lactic acidosis, so it is not the correct first-line treatment in this scenario.

 

Option C. Fructose: Fructose has no role in this situation.

 

Option D. Vitamin B6: While Vitamin B6 has its own important functions, it is not relevant in preventing lactic acidosis caused by thiamine deficiency.

 

Educational objective:


In alcoholic patients, always administer Vitamin B1 (thiamine) before glucose to prevent the worsening of lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: Which is not a substrate-level phosphorylation enzyme?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) PEPCK (Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxykinase)


Substrate-level phosphorylation refers to the direct generation of ATP or GTP from a substrate without the involvement of the electron transport chain. The enzymes responsible for substrate-level phosphorylation generate ATP or GTP during processes like glycolysis and the TCA cycle.

 

PEPCK (Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxykinase) is not involved in substrate-level phosphorylation. It requires GTP for the conversion of oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in gluconeogenesis, but it does not directly produce ATP or GTP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. PG Kinase (Phosphoglycerate Kinase): PG Kinase (Phosphoglycerate Kinase) is a substrate-level phosphorylation enzyme in glycolysis that generates ATP.

 

Option C. Succinate Thiokinase: Succinate Thiokinase (also known as succinyl-CoA synthetase) performs substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle, producing GTP (or ATP, depending on the tissue).

 

Option D. Pyruvate Kinase: Pyruvate Kinase is another substrate-level phosphorylation enzyme in glycolysis, producing ATP.

 

Educational Objective:


PEPCK is not a substrate-level phosphorylation enzyme, as it utilizes GTP but does not generate ATP or GTP directly.

questions.stem: A female neonate born full-term who is failing to thrive and not gaining weight is brought to a paediatrician by her parents. Physical examination showed small head, hypotonia, and low muscle mass. Blood examination showed metabolic acidosis with highly elevated levels of pyruvate, lactate, and alanine. A 6-month history also revealed persistent acidosis which did not go away with thiamine supplementation. The enzyme most likely deficient in this patient is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pyruvate dehydrogenase

 

This neonate presented with physical findings of a small head (microcephaly), hypotonia, low muscle mass, and metabolic acidosis. Blood tests revealed highly elevated levels of pyruvate, lactate, and alanine. The presence of increased pyruvate, lactate, and alanine, along with persistent metabolic acidosis despite thiamine (B1) supplementation, points towards pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency.

 

PDH is a crucial enzyme in the pathway that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, a necessary step for energy production. When PDH is deficient, pyruvate accumulates and is shunted into other pathways, leading to increased production of lactate and alanine, which in turn causes metabolic acidosis. The failure of B1 supplementation to correct the acidosis is consistent with PDH deficiency, as B1 is a cofactor for the enzyme and would not be effective if the enzyme itself is defective.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pyruvate kinase: Pyruvate kinase deficiency results in hemolysis (red blood cell destruction) due to impaired glycolysis, but it does not cause increased levels of pyruvate, lactate, or alanine, and is not associated with metabolic acidosis.

 

Option C. Glucose 6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD): G6PD deficiency also leads to hemolysis, typically after exposure to oxidative stress, and is characterized by the presence of Heinz bodies in red blood cells. This condition does not cause elevated levels of pyruvate, lactate, or alanine, nor does it result in metabolic acidosis.

 

Option D. Pyruvate carboxylase: Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency is associated with hypoglycemia due to its role in gluconeogenesis. This enzyme deficiency does not cause the elevation of pyruvate, lactate, and alanine seen in this patient, nor is it linked to persistent metabolic acidosis without hypoglycemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency leads to elevated levels of pyruvate, lactate, and alanine, causing metabolic acidosis that does not resolve with thiamine supplementation.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male presents with complaints of dizziness, weakness, weariness, and shortness of breath. Blood analysis reported a haemoglobin level of 7 g/dl (male's typical Hb levels >13.5 g/dl) and abnormally low lactate in RBCs. In peripheral blood film (PBF), no Heinz bodies were discovered. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies would be the most likely reason for this patient's anemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pyruvate kinase

 

The patient has hemolysis with a haemoglobin level of 7 g/dl and no Heinz bodies on the peripheral blood film (PBF). These findings point toward pyruvate kinase deficiency. Pyruvate kinase is an important enzyme in glycolysis, and its deficiency leads to the inability of red blood cells to produce enough ATP to maintain their shape, resulting in hemolysis. The absence of Heinz bodies also rules out glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, making pyruvate kinase deficiency the most likely cause.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. G6PD: In G6PD deficiency, Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) would typically be present in the peripheral blood film. Since no Heinz bodies were discovered, G6PD deficiency is less likely. In G6PD deficiency Lactate level is high in RBC.

 

Option C. Hexokinase: Deficiency of hexokinase, an enzyme at the start of the glycolytic pathway, would also impair glycolysis, but it is a rare cause of hemolytic anemia and typically presents with more severe metabolic abnormalities than this case suggests.

 

Option D. Lactate dehydrogenase: Lactate dehydrogenase deficiency would impair the conversion of pyruvate to lactate, but it is not associated with hemolytic anemia. The patient's anemia and absence of Heinz bodies make this option unlikely.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis without the presence of Heinz bodies and is second most common enzyme deficiency leading to hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: All of the following inhibit oxidative phosphorylation except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2,4 dinitrophenol

 

In oxidative phosphorylation, inhibitors of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes will inhibit both oxidation and phosphorylation. Complex inhibitors, such as those affecting complexes I to V, stop the flow of electrons through the chain, which leads to the inhibition of both oxidation and ATP production (phosphorylation). However, uncouplers, such as 2,4 dinitrophenol, allow oxidation to continue while preventing ATP synthesis (phosphorylation).


2,4 dinitrophenol disrupts the proton gradient by allowing protons to pass freely across the mitochondrial membrane without driving ATP synthesis. Therefore, oxidation continues, but phosphorylation is uncoupled from it.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oligomycin: Inhibits ATP synthase (complex V), which stops both oxidation and phosphorylation.

 

Option C. Antimycin: Inhibits complex III of the electron transport chain, halting both oxidation and phosphorylation.

 

Option D. Rotenone: Inhibits complex I of the electron transport chain, preventing both oxidation and phosphorylation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

2,4 dinitrophenol is an uncoupler, allowing oxidation to continue but inhibiting phosphorylation, while inhibitors of electron transport chain complexes block both processes.
