questions.stemHtml: The molecule marked by the blue question mark can be all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acetyl CoA

 

In the diagram, which represents interactions between the liver and muscle, several molecules can serve as intermediates in metabolic cycles such as the Cori cycle and Cahill cycle. These cycles involve the conversion of glucose in the muscle to pyruvate, lactate, or alanine, which are then transported to the liver.

 

In the Cori cycle, glucose is converted into lactate in the muscle, and lactate is transported to the liver, where it can be converted back into glucose.

 

In the Cahill cycle, glucose in the muscle is converted into alanine, which travels to the liver and is converted back to pyruvate, then glucose.

 

Pyruvate, lactate, and alanine are all intermediates in these cycles.

 

However, Acetyl CoA cannot be one of the molecules involved in these cycles because Acetyl CoA is not glucogenic. It cannot be converted back to glucose, as acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle and is used for energy production, not for glucose synthesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pyruvate: Pyruvate is a key intermediate in both the Cori and Cahill cycles, and can easily be converted to lactate or alanine.

 

Option B. Lactate: Lactate is produced from pyruvate in anaerobic glycolysis in muscle and is transported to the liver in the Cori cycle for conversion back to glucose.

 

Option C. Alanine: Alanine is involved in the Cahill cycle, where it is converted back to pyruvate and then to glucose in the liver.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acetyl CoA is not glucogenic and cannot be converted into glucose, unlike pyruvate, lactate, and alanine, which can all participate in cycles that allow conversion back to glucose.

questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy presents to the outpatient clinic with a swollen abdomen and failure to thrive. On examination, his liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin, and he has a doll-like face with chubby cheeks. Laboratory investigations reveal fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia. A liver biopsy demonstrates increased glycogen storage with normal structure. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this patient's clinical presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glucose-6-phosphatase

 

This patient presents with classic symptoms of von Gierke’s disease (glycogen storage disease type I), including hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and increased glycogen storage in the liver with normal structure. The deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase prevents the liver from converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose, resulting in glycogen buildup in the liver and other metabolic disturbances such as fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucokinase: Deficiency of this enzyme affects glucose sensing in the pancreas, but it is not associated with glycogen storage diseases or the specific symptoms seen in this patient.

 

Option B. Muscle glycogen phosphorylase: Deficiency in this enzyme causes McArdle’s disease (glycogen storage disease type V), which presents with muscle weakness and cramps during exercise, not hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, or lactic acidosis.

 

Option D. Phosphofructokinase: This enzyme is essential for glycolysis, and its deficiency is incompatible with life. A deficiency would cause severe energy depletion, leading to intrauterine death, and it is not seen in living individuals.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke’s disease) causes hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia, along with increased glycogen storage in the liver.

questions.stem: Muscles cannot use their glycogen in McArdle's disease due to absence of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glycogen phosphorylase

 

  • McArdle’s disease (Glycogen Storage Disease type V)
  • Cause: Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (also called myophosphorylase).
  • Effect: Muscle cells cannot break down stored glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate → no energy during exercise → exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, myoglobinuria.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Glucose-6-phosphatase 

  • Enzyme that converts glucose-6-phosphate → free glucose.
  • Found mainly in liver & kidney, not in muscle.
  • Deficiency causes Von Gierke’s disease (GSD I) → severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis.
  • Not related to McArdle’s, because muscles don’t use this enzyme at all.

 

Option C. Glycogen-6-phosphatase 

  • There is no enzyme called “glycogen-6-phosphatase”.

 

Option D. G6PD 

  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is part of the pentose phosphate pathway, producing 
  • NADPH to protect RBCs from oxidative damage.
  • Deficiency → hemolytic anemia after oxidative stress (e.g., fava beans, infections, drugs).
    Has no role in glycogen breakdown.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle’s disease) prevents muscles from using their stored glycogen for energy, resulting in muscle weakness and exercise intolerance.

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset jaundice and dark urine. He denies any recent illnesses but mentions that he took an over-the-counter medication for fever two days ago. His family history reveals that his maternal grandfather had a similar episode in the past. Peripheral smear shows the presence of Heinz bodies. Which enzyme deficiency is most consistent with this patient's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)

 

The presence of Heinz bodies on the peripheral smear is a hallmark of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD is responsible for maintaining the integrity of red blood cells by protecting them from oxidative damage. When patients with G6PD deficiency are exposed to oxidative stress, such as certain medications (like the fever medication this patient took), red blood cells are damaged, leading to hemolysis. The resulting hemolysis causes jaundice and dark urine.

 

The patient's family history, with a maternal grandfather having similar episodes, supports G6PD deficiency, which follows an X-linked inheritance pattern. The presence of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) further confirms the diagnosis, as this finding is specific to G6PD deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pyruvate kinase: Deficiency in pyruvate kinase also causes hemolytic anemia, but it is not associated with Heinz bodies. Instead, this deficiency results in chronic hemolysis without an acute episode triggered by oxidative stress.

 

Option B. Hexokinase: Hexokinase deficiency would impair glycolysis, but it is not related to the hemolytic episodes triggered by oxidative stress, nor does it cause Heinz bodies.

 

Option D. Aldolase A: Deficiency in aldolase A affects glycolysis, leading to nonspecific symptoms like fatigue, but it is not associated with hemolysis or Heinz bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

G6PD deficiency leads to hemolysis after exposure to oxidative stress, such as certain medications, and is characterized by the presence of Heinz bodies on a peripheral smear.

questions.stem: Which amino acid is responsible for flexibility of proteins:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glycine

 

Glycine, the smallest and simplest amino acid, is responsible for the flexibility of proteins. Its small size allows it to create bends in the protein structure, providing flexibility. Because of its minimal side chain (just a single hydrogen atom), glycine can fit into tight spaces, especially in regions where the protein bends, contributing to the protein's overall ability to change shape and move.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alanine: While alanine is also a small amino acid, it does not contribute to flexibility in the same way as glycine, as its slightly larger side chain (a methyl group) makes it less suitable for tight bends.

 

Option B. Methionine: Methionine is a larger, sulfur-containing amino acid, which does not contribute to protein flexibility. It is involved more in starting protein synthesis and in some other specific functions, but not in bending.

 

Option D. Glutamate: Glutamate is an amino acid with a large, negatively charged side chain and is involved in protein interactions and signaling, but it does not contribute to flexibility in protein structure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glycine is the smallest amino acid and plays a key role in protein flexibility by allowing bends in the protein structure.

questions.stem: Which of the following has a sulfhydryl group:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cysteine

 

 

Cysteine contains a sulfhydryl group (-SH), which is crucial for the formation of disulfide bonds that stabilize protein structure. The sulfhydryl group allows cysteine to form these disulfide bonds when two cysteine molecules join together, creating cystine, which does not have free sulfhydryl groups but rather a disulfide bond (-S-S-). Methionine contains sulfur, but it is part of a thioether group, not a sulfhydryl group.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cystine: Cystine is formed when two cysteine molecules are linked by a disulfide bond, meaning it does not have a free sulfhydryl group.
 

 

Option C. Methionine: Methionine contains sulfur, but it is in the form of a thioether bond, not a sulfhydryl group.

 

 

Option D. All: This is incorrect because only cysteine has a sulfhydryl (-SH) group.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Only cysteine contains a sulfhydryl group (-SH), which is essential for forming disulfide bonds in proteins.

Ans. C) Adenosine

 

The structure shown in the image is a nucleoside. It contains a purine base (which is a two-ringed structure), and specifically, the purine base here is adenine. The sugar attached to this purine base is ribose (since both hydroxyl groups are present at positions 2 and 3), which confirms that this is a nucleoside, not a deoxyribonucleoside.

 

Since there is no phosphate group attached, this cannot be an adenine nucleotide, which would require the presence of phosphate groups in addition to the sugar and nitrogenous base.

 

Therefore, the correct identification of this structure is adenosine, which is a nucleoside composed of adenine and ribose.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cytidine: This would have a pyrimidine base (single ring) attached to ribose, but the structure shown has two rings, indicating it is a purine.

 

Option B. Cytosine: Cytosine is a pyrimidine base, but the structure shown belongs to a purine.

 

Option D. Adenine nucleotide: A nucleotide would have a phosphate group attached, which is not present in the structure shown.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The structure of adenosine consists of the nitrogenous base adenine attached to a ribose sugar, making it a nucleoside. The absence of phosphate distinguishes it from an adenine nucleotide.
